alt: A float is formatted with the spec greater-than 7 point 2 f. First the decimals are fixed at two. Then the width of 7 is applied, with padding spaces shown as dots on the left. A number already wider than 7 gets no padding. The last step shows the printed field.

steps.caption: `x` holds 3.14159. The spec `>7.2f` has three parts: `.2f` for the decimals, `7` for the width, and `>` for the alignment. Python applies them in that order.
`.2f` turns the float into text with exactly two digits after the point: 3.14. That text is 4 characters long.
`7` asks for a field at least 7 wide. The text is 4, so 3 padding spaces are needed, drawn here as dots. `>` puts them on the left, which lines the text up against the right edge.
`print` shows [   3.14]. The brackets belong to the f-string, so you can see where the field begins and ends.
`x` holds 12345.6. The spec `>7.2f` has three parts: `.2f` for the decimals, `7` for the width, and `>` for the alignment. Python applies them in that order.
`.2f` turns the float into text with exactly two digits after the point: 12345.60. That text is 8 characters long.
`7` asks for a field at least 7 wide. The text is already 8, so no padding is added. A width is a minimum: Python never cuts a number short to fit it.
`print` shows [12345.60]. The brackets belong to the f-string, so you can see where the field begins and ends.
`x` holds 7.0. The spec `>7.2f` has three parts: `.2f` for the decimals, `7` for the width, and `>` for the alignment. Python applies them in that order.
`.2f` turns the float into text with exactly two digits after the point: 7.00. That text is 4 characters long.
`7` asks for a field at least 7 wide. The text is 4, so 3 padding spaces are needed, drawn here as dots. `>` puts them on the left, which lines the text up against the right edge.
`print` shows [   7.00]. The brackets belong to the f-string, so you can see where the field begins and ends.
